title: Pasture mealybugs have killed off huge swaths of grasses in the Southeast
description:
From Texas Standard

An invasive insect that's tough to detect and eliminate poses a multi-billion dollar threat to the agricultural economy — adding another stressor to farmers already stretched by high costs.

AILSA CHANG, HOST: Many farmers and ranchers are being pinched by the high cost of fertilizer and diesel fuel. Now, some southern states are also dealing with a new pest, one that is difficult to detect. Michael Marks of the Texas Standard reports.MICHAEL MARKS, BYLINE: In July, Texas A&M AgriLife pest specialist Danielle Sekula got a strange call from a farmer she works with. While mowing hay, his machine looked like it caught on fire, but there were no flames.DANIELLE SEKULA: I got called out because there was hay balers that - like, there was white smoke coming out.MARKS: Sekula works with farmers near the Rio Grande Valley. This audio is from a video of what she saw...(SOUNDBITE OF MOWER RUNNING)MARKS: ...Thick, grayish vapor billowing out of a mower rolling through a hayfield. The farmers did not know what was going on. Sekula did.SEKULA: And they're like, it's not on fire. And I was like, oh, man, that's pasture mealybug.MARKS: The field was so infested with these minuscule insects that their chopped-up remnants looked like smoke coming out of the mower. Pasture mealybugs appeared in South Texas in 2022. They've since spread into Louisiana, Georgia and Florida.DAVID KERNS: Well, we don't know a whole lot about them.MARKS: David Kerns is an associate head of the entomology department with Texas A&M University. He's been helping lead the charge against pasture mealybug.KERNS: They do like it hot and humid, and particularly, they like thick, tall grass.MARKS: Kerns estimated that pasture mealybug could cost Texas farmers and ranchers $2 billion per year. They are so small that some people, like William Steubing, mistake infestations for some kind of white mold.WILLIAM STEUBING: They're easy to overlook. Boy, the first time I looked at them - if I would have looked at that and not had somebody tell me what it was, I would have thought it was a fungus.MARKS: Steubing and his family run cattle in Central Texas on land that's been in his family since the 1890s. His mother spotted the problem first, when she noticed portions of a pasture starting to die.STEUBING: You know, you'll get bald spots in your pasture here and there. That's not a big thing. But there were physically dead plants in there.MARKS: Mealybugs weaken grass by injecting a toxin into the plant and sucking out its sap. The affected grass will often turn yellow, then red or purple, then die. And the pests don't just feed on hay. Julien Beuzelin is a University of Florida entomologist who works with sugarcane.JULIEN BEUZELIN: I really believe that if you scout hard enough, you will find at least one mealybug in every single field.MARKS: Florida farmers first identified the pasture mealybug in late May, after most of the year's sugarcane had already been harvested. But Beuzelin said that the crop that's currently growing is suffering from the pest.BEUZELIN: The integrity of the stalk - it is not the same. The stalks become rubbery. So again, you have an insect that can be devastating.MARKS: The Environmental Protection Agency has approved several pesticides to fight the insects but none are a silver bullet. And according to David Kerns, the Texas A&M entomologist, they cost more than some farmers want to pay.KERNS: I mean, I wish I could halve the price or something, but we can't.MARKS: Researchers like Kerns and Beuzelin are now focusing on learning more about the pasture mealybug itself, as well as whether certain crops may be more resistant to its effects.For NPR News, I'm Michael Marks.(SOUNDBITE OF POST MALONE SONG, "CHEMICAL") Copyright © 2026 NPR.
